Wednesday was a broad relief rally led by tech. The S&P 500 closed at 7619.38 (+98.45, +1.31%) and the Nasdaq Composite at 25466.19 (+1.60%). Info Tech jumped 2.71% on the day but is still -10.31% over 1 month. The VIX fell 1.97 to 17.49 (-10.12%), and Europe (Euro Stoxx 50 +1.04%) and Japan (Nikkei +1.31%) joined in. Sentiment improved from the prior session, but the internals are less convincing than the tape. (1) TECH PHASE MODEL: the basket is still in Phase 1 ('initial drop, credit calm'), 26 days from its peak, with a basket drawdown of -13.31% vs -17.92% for the 2000 basket on the same day. The breadth signpost IS TRIGGERED: 64.3% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs, against a 50% line. The 6-month P2/P3 odds rose 6.2pp vs the prior day. The phase model puts the chance of ever reaching Phase 2 or worse at 0.40 over 6 months and 0.564 over 12 months (model estimates, not certainties). SOX is -27.81% from its 52-week high, 2.19 points from the -30% AI-infra signpost. The rally-watch conditions are on (VIX spike-and-turn with calm credit), but historically half of these set-ups were traps. (2) HY CONTAGION: the Caa–B gap is 790bp, in the 99.76th percentile of 5 years (5y average 419.5bp). It is +80bp over 1 month and +217bp over 3 months, and the widest since 2020-04-15. So far the stress has not spread up the ladder: single-B is 308bp (-21bp 1w, +15bp 1m), Ba 189bp (+4bp 1m), IG 88bp, and the B–Ba gap is at its 5y median (50th pctl). The 63-day Caa/B correlation has climbed from 0.34 three months ago to 0.65, back near its 0.69 5y median. That is the channel to watch, but it is descriptive, not a signal. (3) AI BACKSTOP: CoreWeave 5Y CDS fell 54.3bp on the day to 1167.4bp. It is still only 27.1bp below the 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record and has kept 96% of its run from the 452bp June low. Nvidia CDS edged up 3.35bp to 144.0bp. On today's evidence the market is only partly buying Nvidia's backstop of the neoclouds: the guarantor's CDS is not tightening, and CoreWeave's own risk is pricing near its worst levels. Rates were quiet in the US (10Y 4.992%), but the JGB 10Y jumped 10.7bp to 2.803%.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 421.13 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD's front month is at 421.13 cents/gal, at the 99.0th percentile of its history with a z-score of 2.64. The curve is in steep backwardation: it falls to 340.6 by the 12th month and 263.1 by the 36th, so the market is paying a big premium for prompt barrels. A crack spread of 90.3446 $/bbl (z 4.65) points the same way. The squeeze is concentrated in the front of the curve and is not a broad repricing of diesel. All five gauges are at extremes and all signal SELL, so the main questions are timing and how much room to give the stops.

ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil (Europe/Asia Diesel) — current: 1316.00 $/tonne vs Brent

ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil is trading at 1316.0 $/tonne, a 99.2nd-percentile level (z 2.66). Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.59 vol points (33th percentile of the 66 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 92.4 (66th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 76bp (flatter by 12bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 41 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 62/100 — Sticky, not re-accelerating broadly. Core PCE at 3.12% and core sticky CPI near 3.06% keep underlying inflation about a point above target. The median, trimmed-mean and sticky measures sit in the upper-middle of their history and mostly point rising (see the computed Core-Trend Sub-Score). The Dallas Fed distribution shows 26.8% of the PCE basket rising faster than 5% (16.6% above 10%), against 25.6% falling. That is a polarized basket rather than broad-based acceleration. Market inflation expectations are anchored (5y breakeven 2.2595%, 1y 1.9922%) and wage growth is moderate (AHE 3.1%). The result is a 'higher-for-longer' backdrop that limits how fast the Fed can ease.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
9 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 58/100
Today looks more like an early-bust phase than a March-2000 peak. Equity froth is far below 2000: Nasdaq trailing P/E is 39.85x vs 175x at the peak (16% of the way), stretch vs the 200DMA 3%, and semis P/E at 42% of peak. Late-cycle catalyst and regime gauges are at or past 2000 conditions: IG credit tightness 127%, Baa–10Y tightness 172%, commodities-vs-equities 200%, loose financial conditions (NFCI) 148%, VIX complacency 181%. Sentiment signposts are not euphoric: AAII 14%, put/call 36%, confidence 31%. The phase model places the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm). Its estimates: stays in Phase 1 at 0.852 over 1 month and 0.546 over 6 months; ever reaching Phase 2 or worse is 0.12 at 1 month, 0.40 at 6 months, 0.564 at 12 months and 0.618 at 24 months. These are model estimates, not certainties. The breadth signpost has triggered, and the 6m P2/P3 odds rose 6.2pp vs the prior day.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (40x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analog fits on the credit side, not on valuation. Prices are not stretched (Nasdaq only 1.37% above its 200DMA), but the drawdown is underway: basket -13.31% from its peak and 64.3% of names more than 20% off their highs. Meanwhile credit and financial conditions are as loose as or looser than in 2000. The regime models read equity as 'volatile bull' (0.913) with credit 'calm' (0.969). A Phase-2 move would require HY OAS to widen about 128bp to 448bp or Baa–10Y about 45bp to 195bp. The CCC gap and CoreWeave CDS are where that would show first. The rally-watch set-up is on (VIX spike from 28.2 then turn to 17.5, HY only +8bp over 10 days). Historically half of these were traps: about 10.7% gains over ~17.5 days, vs about 32.4% over ~106.5 days for real rallies. The historical phase-conditional tilt at this mix favoured gold, Treasury duration and IG credit over mega-cap growth, developed international and EM. The analyst-estimate inputs (concentration ~38%, CAPE ~38x, market cap/GDP ~210%, LT EPS growth expectations 65/100) are approximate, from general knowledge, and were not verified by search in this run. IPO froth (60/100) reflects the planned Anthropic offering of $75B+, which could be the largest IPO ever.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

INFERENCE: most likely a hold at the next FOMC meeting. Core PCE is 3.12% with sticky measures rising, labor is firm (unemployment 4.1%, claims 189k), and reporting says Warsh must persuade a split committee to cut. A cut is possible if credit stress spreads, but it is not our base case.

~1 YEAR

INFERENCE: a gradual easing bias, in line with his record of arguing that a smaller balance sheet makes room for lower policy rates. Balance-sheet changes are likely slow and committee-driven. Expect a regime change in communications: less forward guidance, a framework review via his task forces, and no personal SEP forecasts.

Warsh chaired his first meeting in June 2026. He declined to submit his own Summary of Economic Projections and launched five task forces covering communications, the balance sheet, the inflation framework, data and productivity. Analysts (PIMCO, Gulf Times/Reuters) describe a 'regime change' that needs patience and consensus. Pre-confirmation analysis expected him to favor at least the two 2026 cuts in the Dec-2025 projections, but notes he must convince most of the 11 other voters. The Fed had already stopped balance-sheet runoff and was buying bills for liquidity, so aggressive QT looks unlikely near term. The near-term and 1-year calls above are our inferences from his record and today's data, not reported Fed decisions.

Sources: PIMCO – Under a Warsh Fed, expect a thoughtful policy approach · Gulf Times – Warsh's Fed regime change may require patience, consensus · Yahoo Finance – Kevin Warsh's Fed record: what it signals for interest rates · MarketScreener – A regime change: Kevin Warsh, the man who wants to revolutionize the Fed · Pepperstone – Warsh nomination: implications for rate cuts, balance sheet and communications

Descriptive regime read, not advice and not a recommendation to trade. Rule results are simulations on one market history (3x daily returns rebuilt from index data, 1-day lag, costs), and the exits (+10% target, 5-day pause) were chosen after testing a few values on that same history, so treat them as in-sample. The trend+vol engine is a drawdown control, not proven timing skill (trendvol TRENDVOL.md § CORRECTION). Credit widening = 63-day change past the monitor_spread triggers (Baa +0.15pp, HY OAS +0.50pp, IG OAS +0.15pp); as a standalone overlay that rule failed its pre-registered gates. Leveraged and inverse ETFs reset daily and decay.
